title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
AI was used to create a fake news article impersonating real public figures, the Reserve Bank governor and a finance presenter, in order to fraudulently promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The impersonation took place in a text-based article, not a video or audio deepfake. This failure is deployment without verification: the fake article appeared online designed to deceive readers into trusting false endorsements of an investment scheme.

This category of fraud relies on AI systems generating convincing text or images that audiences have no way to verify without checking original sources. Catching it would have required readers to confirm the interview through official media outlets or the central bank before acting on it. It would also have required the platform hosting the article to verify claims before publication, or to authenticate that the quoted figures had actually consented to their apparent endorsement.

What is not established: whether the AI system was purpose-built for fraud or a general tool misused by scammers, or what specific AI technology created the article.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article falsely portrayed Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. This fabricated story never occurred but was designed to promote the unregistered trading platform. The incident exemplifies a rapidly growing category of investment fraud that uses artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfake content featuring well-known Australian figures including politicians, business leaders, and media personalities.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission data reveals these scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent. Last year, the regulator removed 19,400 scams overall, up 182 percent, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing attempts. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake websites, news articles, testimonials, and social media advertisements to trick people into providing personal details and money. ASIC urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers and to be skeptical of investment opportunities featuring celebrity endorsements, as polished content does not guarantee legitimacy.
